pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 3: Growing: a problem.*

I came back after breakfast expecting a small green shoot. What I found was a mistake.

The pea was already a foot tall, its stem crooked and the color of bruised skin, twitching without any wind to explain it. Another inch grew while I blinked, then two more when I blinked again. Gherkin was eating a lettuce leaf, taking one bite every ten seconds and chewing with the deliberate slowness of a machine that had been told to stop.

"Mm," he said.

I waited.

"Ah," he finished, fifteen seconds later.

I stared at the vine, which was wrapping around the brass trowel I had left behind until the metal bent like a sad, twisted spoon.

"I forgot," I said. "I didn't say a true thing."

Gherkin swallowed the lettuce. "Mm. The garden... does not forgive... lies."

"It wasn't a lie," I said. "It was an omission."

"Same thing," Gherkin said. "To the root."
pages.image: A thin 11-year-old girl with brown skin, round glasses, and a low black bun with a green pencil through it, stands in a garden staring at a rapidly growing, crooked blue-green pea vine; an old tortoise with a mossy shell eats a lettuce leaf in the foreground.

pages.text:
The vine was winning. It had wrapped the garden fork in a tight spiral and climbed the pear tree, which now leaned dangerously to the left. It stretched across the brick path, dragging the rusted seed tin behind it like a heavy bag of sugar being pulled by a dog.

I pulled out my tape measure. It felt like a weapon, or a tool, or both. "Stop," I commanded the vine.

It grew four centimeters. I measured it. Sixty centimeters. I breathed in, then out, and measured again. Ninety centimeters. The tin was now three inches from the hedge.

"Please," I said. "I am trying to help."

The vine whipped around and slapped the tape measure out of my hand. It landed in a puddle. I picked it up, dripping, and watched it reach one meter twenty. It had found the bench. It was trying to eat it.

I measured the distance to the hedge. Two meters. Then one and a half. Then one.

I was losing. I could feel the speed of it in my stomach, a heavy, sinking feeling, like dropping a stone into a deep well and waiting for the splash.
pages.image: A chaotic garden scene where a long, spiraling blue-green pea vine wraps around a garden fork and a pear tree, pulling a rusted metal tin across brick pavers; a small, thin girl with round glasses holds a wet tape measure, looking alarmed.

pages.text:
"How do I stop it?" I asked, watching the green chaos spread.

Gherkin was still chewing a piece of lettuce. He lifted one claw and pointed it at the vine. "Say... a true word."

"I did," I said, my voice cracking. "I said I am trying to help. That is true."

"The vine... grows," Gherkin said slowly. "It needs... a truth... that costs."

I tried again, keeping my voice steady. "I am patient."

The vine snapped up three inches in a single jerk. Thorns appeared along the stem. They were sharp and black, exactly like the plastic tips of broken ballpoint pens.

"I like it here," I tried next.

More thorns erupted. The vine wrapped tighter around the fork, and the metal made a high-pitched squealing sound, similar to a school bell being rubbed with sandpaper.

"I am fine," I said, because I was an eleven-year-old girl and "I am fine" was the safest sentence in the world.

A small pea flower appeared on the tip of the vine. It was perfect, with white petals and a yellow center. Then it wilted, turned brown, and fell off to hit the ground with a tiny, sad thump.

The vine hissed, sounding exactly like a kettle boiling over.

I sat down on the bench, which was vibrating under my jacket. I did not want to look at the vine. I wanted to go home and hide in the bath with the taps running, letting the water wash away the smell of failure.
pages.image: A girl in an oversized denim jacket sits on a wooden bench, looking exhausted and frustrated; a large, thorny blue-green pea vine looms over her, with a small wilted flower on the ground nearby; an old tortoise watches from a patch of grass.

pages.text:
The vine was coiling around my ankle. It was not hurting me. It was just holding me. Waiting.

I looked at the hedge. Two inches away. The tin would break. The seeds inside would spill out. And I would have to explain that I had broken a rule because I forgot a sentence.

My throat was tight. I swallowed. It felt like swallowing a pebble.

"I didn't want to move here," I said.

The vine stopped twitching.

"I was really angry at Mama and Baba," I said, and my voice was small, smaller than I wanted it to be. "And I still am. A bit."

The bench hummed. It was a low, warm sound, like a bee trapped in a jar.

The vine shuddered. It began to shrink. Not suddenly. Slowly. The thorns retracted. The crooked stem straightened. It pulled back from the fork, the tree, the tin. It retreated into the soil, leaf by leaf, until all that was left was a small, neat pea sprout.

It was about the length of my hand. It was green. It was alive.

I looked at my hands. They were shaking. I had said it out loud. I had said it to a tortoise. But it was out.
pages.image: A close-up of a small, healthy green pea sprout in the soil, looking neat and strong; in the background, a blurred view of a wooden bench and a girl's hands, which are clasped together tightly.

pages.text:
Gherkin blinked. It took eight seconds.

"Mm," he said. "There. Now... it's growing."

I stared at the sprout. "It's tiny."

"Three weeks," Gherkin said. "To flower."

I groaned. It was a loud, ugly sound. I did not care who heard. Three weeks meant I would have to come back every day, water it, and wait.

The bench hummed again, softer now.

I stood up, my legs feeling wobbly, and looked at the sprout, then at the tin, which was safe. I picked up my tape measure. I did not put it back in my pocket. I held it in my hand.

I walked to the gap in the fence. I paused.

I wanted to go home and hide from the boxes and the list and the dinosaur. But I also wanted to come back. I wanted to see if the sprout had grown two centimeters.

I climbed over the fence. My breath was in my chest, tight and full. I had promised, without deciding to, to be here tomorrow.

And for the first time in nine days, I wanted to keep it.
pages.image: A small girl with brown skin and round glasses climbs over a chain-link fence, looking back with a mix of relief and determination; a small green pea sprout is visible in the garden behind her; the setting is late afternoon with soft light.
